title: Multi-Account Architecture & AWS Organizations
summary: AWS Organizations lets you centrally manage billing and policy across many AWS accounts, grouped into Organizational Units (OUs) that mirror your business or environment structure (e.g. Security, Infrastructure, Workloads/Prod, Workloads/Dev). The management (root) account should hold no workloads — it exists purely for consolidated billing and org-wide policy.
lab: Draft an OU hierarchy isolating Dev, Staging, and Production accounts under a Workloads OU, with a separate Security OU for log-archive and audit accounts.

questions.q: A company wants a dedicated account that only aggregates CloudTrail logs from every other account and cannot be modified by workload teams. Where should this account live?
options: Directly under the root, alongside Production
In a dedicated Security OU with a restrictive SCP
Inside the Workloads/Prod OU for proximity to the data it audits
questions.explanation: Log-archive/audit accounts belong in a dedicated Security OU protected by SCPs that deny deletion or modification of logging resources, isolated from workload OUs.

questions.q: Why should the AWS Organizations management account never run workloads?
options: It has a lower service quota by default
SCPs cannot be applied to it, so it should be kept empty to reduce blast radius and support least privilege
It is billed at a premium rate
questions.explanation: The management account is immune to SCPs, so best practice keeps it workload-free to minimize risk — it should only handle billing, Organizations, and org-wide services like IAM Identity Center.

title: Service Control Policy (SCP) Mechanics
summary: SCPs are org-wide permission guardrails: they set the maximum available permissions for accounts in an OU but never grant access by themselves — an IAM identity still needs an allow. The default FullAWSAccess SCP allows everything until you attach explicit Deny statements. Region-restriction SCPs must exempt global services (IAM, Route 53, CloudFront, Support) or you will break account operations.
lab: Write and validate a region-restriction SCP that denies all actions outside two approved regions while exempting IAM, Route 53, CloudFront, and Support.

questions.q: A developer has an IAM policy granting s3:*, but an SCP on their OU denies s3:DeleteBucket. What happens if they call DeleteBucket?
options: It succeeds because IAM policies take precedence
It is denied — SCPs set the ceiling and an explicit Deny always wins
It succeeds only in the management account
It depends on the S3 bucket policy
questions.explanation: The effective permission is the intersection of IAM and SCP; an explicit Deny in either always overrides an Allow.

title: AWS Control Tower & Account Factory
summary: Control Tower automates a multi-account landing zone: it provisions a management account, log-archive account, and audit account, and enforces mandatory and elective guardrails (implemented as SCPs and AWS Config rules) across enrolled OUs. Account Factory for Terraform (AFT) extends this with pipeline-driven account provisioning for teams already standardized on Terraform.
lab: Review how Account Factory for Terraform (AFT) layers custom account customizations on top of Control Tower's baseline guardrails.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a mandatory and an elective Control Tower guardrail?
options: Mandatory guardrails cannot be disabled and are always enforced; elective guardrails are optional best practices you can turn on/off
Elective guardrails only apply to the management account
questions.explanation: Mandatory guardrails (e.g. disallow root user access keys) are always active; elective and strongly recommended guardrails can be enabled per OU based on your governance needs.

title: IAM Identity Center (AWS SSO) & Federation
summary: IAM Identity Center centralizes human access across all accounts in an Organization via permission sets mapped to SAML federation from an external IdP (Entra ID, Okta) or its own built-in directory. Permission sets translate to an IAM role provisioned automatically into each assigned account, avoiding long-lived per-account IAM users.
lab: Configure a permission set granting ReadOnlyAccess in Production and PowerUserAccess in Dev, then assign it to a federated group.

questions.q: An enterprise wants engineers to log in once via their corporate Okta and assume the correct role in any of 40 AWS accounts without individual IAM users. What is the best-practice solution?
options: Create an IAM user per engineer per account
IAM Identity Center with SAML federation from Okta and permission sets
Share a single root-account access key
questions.explanation: IAM Identity Center is purpose-built for centralized SSO across an Organization, provisioning short-lived federated roles instead of long-lived IAM users.

title: IAM Permission Boundaries & STS
summary: A permission boundary is a managed policy that caps the maximum permissions an IAM entity can ever have, even if its attached policies are broader — commonly used so a delegated admin can create roles without being able to escalate beyond the boundary. STS issues short-lived credentials via AssumeRole, AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity (OIDC federation, e.g. EKS IRSA), and AssumeRoleWithSAML.
lab: Create an IAM delegate-admin role that can create new IAM roles, but only ones scoped inside a permission boundary that blocks IAM/Organizations changes.

questions.q: A delegated admin role can create IAM roles for developers. How do you prevent them from creating a role with AdministratorAccess?
options: Attach a Deny statement to every developer role individually
Require the delegated admin to set a permission boundary on every role they create, capping maximum permissions
questions.explanation: Enforcing a mandatory permission boundary (via a condition requiring iam:PermissionsBoundary on CreateRole) is the standard pattern to prevent privilege escalation by delegated admins.

title: Resource Access Manager (RAM) & VPC Sharing
summary: AWS RAM lets a central network account share resources — most commonly VPC subnets, Transit Gateways, and Route 53 Resolver rules — with other accounts in the Organization, so application accounts launch resources into a centrally managed network without owning the VPC themselves.
lab: Share a centralized VPC's private subnets across three application accounts via RAM and verify each account can launch EC2 instances into the shared subnet.

questions.q: A company wants every application account to use a common, centrally managed VPC without each account owning its own VPC. What is the mechanism?
options: VPC Peering between every pair of accounts
Share subnets from a central VPC using AWS RAM
Transit Gateway alone, with each account keeping its own VPC
Copy the VPC configuration manually into every account
questions.explanation: RAM subnet sharing lets many accounts launch resources into subnets owned by a single central VPC — reducing IP management and networking overhead versus peering or per-account VPCs.

title: Week 1 Synthesis & Multi-Account Drill
summary: Consolidate the week: multi-account landing zone design, SCP guardrails, Control Tower automation, centralized SSO, and shared networking. Focus on how these pieces compose into a single enterprise governance model.
lab: Complete 15 scenario questions spanning AWS Organizations, SCPs, Control Tower, and IAM Identity Center.

questions.q: Which combination best represents a mature multi-account governance baseline?
options: A single flat account with IAM users per team
Control Tower landing zone + OU-based SCPs + IAM Identity Center SSO + RAM-shared networking
SCPs only, with no account separation
questions.explanation: Enterprise governance combines automated account provisioning (Control Tower), policy guardrails (SCPs), centralized identity (Identity Center), and shared network plumbing (RAM/Transit Gateway).

title: Transit Gateway (TGW) Core Routing
summary: Transit Gateway is a regional network transit hub connecting VPCs and on-prem networks via a hub-and-spoke model, replacing an unmanageable full mesh of VPC peering. Each attachment associates with one TGW route table and propagates routes into others, enabling fine-grained segmentation (e.g. isolating a shared-services VPC from production VPCs).
lab: Build a hub-and-spoke VPC topology connecting three isolated VPCs through a single Transit Gateway with segmented route tables.

questions.q: You need Dev and Prod VPCs to both reach a Shared-Services VPC, but never reach each other. How do you design TGW route tables?
options: A single flat TGW route table with all routes propagated
Separate TGW route tables for Dev and Prod that each only propagate Shared-Services routes, with no propagation between Dev and Prod
VPC Peering directly between Dev and Prod
Use only Security Groups to block traffic
questions.explanation: TGW route table segmentation is the standard way to implement network isolation between spokes while still allowing shared access to common services.

title: Transit Gateway Peering & Multi-Region
summary: TGW peering connects Transit Gateways across regions over the AWS backbone (not the public internet), but peering attachments do not support route propagation — routes must be added statically. MTU across inter-region TGW peering is capped at 1500 bytes.
lab: Route traffic between us-east-1 and us-west-2 VPCs through peered Transit Gateways with manually configured static routes.

questions.q: After creating a TGW peering attachment between two regions, spoke VPCs still cannot reach each other. What is most likely missing?
options: Route propagation is disabled for peering attachments — static routes must be added manually
The TGWs are in different Availability Zones
Peering doesn't support cross-region traffic at all
Security groups always block inter-region traffic
questions.explanation: Unlike VPC/TGW attachments, TGW peering attachments require manually created static routes in each TGW route table — automatic propagation is not supported.

title: AWS Network Firewall & Centralized Egress
summary: AWS Network Firewall provides stateful and stateless traffic inspection using Suricata-compatible rules, typically deployed in a centralized inspection VPC that all egress/ingress traffic is routed through via Transit Gateway and route table tricks (appliance VPC pattern).
lab: Route all outbound internet traffic from spoke VPCs through a centralized inspection VPC running AWS Network Firewall.

questions.q: What is the standard pattern for forcing all internet-bound traffic from multiple VPCs through a single AWS Network Firewall?
options: Deploy Network Firewall independently in every VPC
Centralized inspection VPC attached to Transit Gateway, with spoke route tables directing 0.0.0.0/0 to the TGW
Use only NACLs on each spoke subnet
Network Firewall cannot inspect cross-VPC traffic
questions.explanation: The centralized/hub inspection VPC pattern routes all spoke egress through TGW into a shared Network Firewall, avoiding per-VPC firewall duplication and cost.

title: Direct Connect (DX) & DX Gateway
summary: Direct Connect provides a dedicated private network connection into AWS, using Private VIFs for single-VPC access, Transit VIFs for connecting to a Transit Gateway (and many VPCs), and Public VIFs for public AWS service endpoints. Resilience requires redundant connections/locations with BGP failover, not a single link.
lab: Design a redundant Direct Connect architecture using two connections at different DX locations with active/passive BGP path preference (AS PATH prepending or local preference).

questions.q: A company needs the highest resiliency Direct Connect design for a mission-critical workload. What should they provision?
options: Two DX connections at two different DX locations, each terminating on separate devices, with BGP failover and a VPN backup
One DX connection plus a second identical connection at the same location
Public VIF only, since it's cheaper
questions.explanation: AWS's resiliency model for DX requires diversity across DX locations and devices, plus BGP-based failover; a VPN backup adds an additional layer for the rare case both DX paths fail.

title: AWS Route 53 Resolver (Hybrid DNS)
summary: Route 53 Resolver enables hybrid DNS: Inbound endpoints let on-prem resolvers query AWS-hosted private hosted zones; Outbound endpoints + forwarding rules let AWS resources resolve on-prem domain names, routed over Direct Connect or VPN.
lab: Configure a conditional forwarding rule sending queries for corp.internal to an on-prem DNS server via a Resolver outbound endpoint.

questions.q: On-prem servers need to resolve names in a private Route 53 hosted zone. What do you configure?
options: A Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint, with on-prem DNS forwarding queries to it
questions.explanation: Inbound endpoints expose AWS private DNS to on-prem resolvers; outbound endpoints do the reverse (AWS resolving on-prem names).

title: AWS PrivateLink & VPC Peering Comparison
summary: PrivateLink exposes a service in one VPC/account to another via an ENI-backed Interface Endpoint, without VPC peering, route table changes, or overlapping-CIDR conflicts — ideal for exposing a single microservice across many consumer accounts. Gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB only) use route table entries instead of ENIs and are free.
lab: Expose an internal microservice across accounts via a PrivateLink endpoint service, avoiding VPC peering and IP overlap issues entirely.

questions.q: Two companies with overlapping CIDR ranges (both 10.0.0.0/16) need one to consume a specific API hosted in the other's VPC. What connectivity option works despite the overlap?
questions.explanation: PrivateLink only requires ENI-level connectivity in the consumer VPC and never merges route tables/CIDRs, so it works fine even with fully overlapping IP ranges — unlike peering or TGW.

title: Week 2 Synthesis & Networking Lab Exam
summary: Consolidate hybrid connectivity: when to use TGW vs peering vs PrivateLink, DX resiliency patterns, and hybrid DNS resolution. This is one of the highest-weight topic clusters on the exam.
lab: Complete 20 scenario questions on hybrid connectivity, Transit Gateway design, and DNS routing.

questions.q: When should you choose PrivateLink over Transit Gateway for cross-account connectivity?
options: When you need full bidirectional network-level reachability between VPCs
When exposing a single specific service to many consumers without merging networks or worrying about CIDR overlap
questions.explanation: PrivateLink is service-level exposure (one service, many consumers, no shared routing); TGW is network-level connectivity for broad multi-VPC/on-prem routing.

title: Amazon ECS Fargate Architecture & Task Definitions
summary: Fargate runs ECS (or EKS) tasks without managing EC2 instances — each task gets its own isolated compute allocation defined by a task definition (CPU/memory, container images, IAM task role, network mode). awsvpc networking gives each task its own ENI and security group.
lab: Configure an ALB path-based routing rule in front of an ECS Fargate service with a dedicated task IAM role scoped to least privilege.

questions.q: Why does Fargate's awsvpc network mode assign each task its own ENI?
options: To give each task an isolated security group and IP, avoiding port-mapping conflicts of bridge mode
questions.explanation: awsvpc mode gives every task first-class networking — its own ENI, private IP, and security group — enabling fine-grained per-task security instead of shared host-level rules.

title: Amazon EKS Architecture & Managed Node Groups vs Fargate
summary: EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane as a managed service; worker capacity comes from self-managed nodes, managed node groups (AWS-managed Auto Scaling Groups), or Fargate profiles (per-pod serverless, no node management, but no DaemonSets and higher per-pod cost).
lab: Compare a managed node group vs an EKS Fargate profile for a namespace with unpredictable, bursty batch workloads.

questions.q: A workload requires DaemonSets for log collection on every node. Which EKS compute option should you avoid?
options: EKS Fargate profiles — Fargate does not support DaemonSets
questions.explanation: Fargate pods run in isolated micro-VMs with no shared node, so DaemonSets (which require a persistent per-node agent) are not supported.

title: Auto Scaling Groups — Lifecycle Hooks & Warm Pools
summary: Lifecycle hooks pause an instance in Pending:Wait or Terminating:Wait so you can run bootstrap/drain scripts (e.g. deregister from a load balancer, flush logs) before it enters service or terminates. Warm pools keep pre-initialized, stopped instances ready to scale out fast without full boot/bootstrap latency.
lab: Configure a lifecycle hook on instance termination that drains in-flight connections and uploads final logs to S3 before the instance is terminated.

questions.q: An application takes 4 minutes to bootstrap before it can serve traffic, causing scale-out to lag demand spikes. What reduces this latency?
options: Use a Warm Pool of pre-initialized stopped instances so scale-out promotes them instead of booting from cold
Add a lifecycle hook on launch
questions.explanation: Warm pools keep instances pre-initialized (stopped or running) so the ASG can bring them into service in seconds instead of re-running the full bootstrap sequence.

title: Application Load Balancer — Advanced Routing & Target Groups
summary: ALB supports path-based, host-based, and header/query-string routing rules to multiple target groups, plus weighted target groups for blue/green and canary traffic shifting, and Lambda targets for serverless backends.
lab: Configure ALB weighted target groups to shift 10% of production traffic to a new (green) task set for a canary release.

questions.q: What ALB feature enables a canary deployment shifting a small percentage of traffic to a new version before full cutover?
options: Weighted target groups on a single listener rule
questions.explanation: Weighted target groups let one routing rule split traffic by percentage across two target groups — the standard ALB-native canary/blue-green mechanism.

title: AWS Lambda Advanced — Concurrency, VPC Networking & Event Source Mapping
summary: Reserved concurrency caps (and guarantees) a function's max concurrent executions; provisioned concurrency pre-warms execution environments to eliminate cold starts. Event source mapping polls streaming/queue sources (Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams, SQS) and invokes Lambda in batches, with per-source concurrency and error-handling behavior (partial batch failures, DLQs).
lab: Configure provisioned concurrency for a latency-sensitive Lambda and reserved concurrency to protect a downstream RDS instance from connection exhaustion.

questions.q: A Lambda function reading from Kinesis is overwhelming a downstream RDS database with connections during traffic spikes. What limits this safely?
options: Set reserved concurrency on the function to cap max concurrent executions
questions.explanation: Reserved concurrency caps how many instances of the function can run simultaneously, directly bounding the number of concurrent downstream connections.

title: Serverless Architectures — Step Functions & API Gateway
summary: Step Functions orchestrates multi-step workflows (Lambda, ECS tasks, human approval waits) with built-in retry/catch and Standard (exactly-once, long-running, auditable) vs Express (high-throughput, at-least-once, cheaper) workflow types. API Gateway fronts these with REST/HTTP APIs, request validation, and native service integrations that bypass Lambda entirely for simple pass-through.
lab: Design a Step Functions Standard workflow with a human-approval wait state and automatic retry/catch on a downstream Lambda failure.

questions.q: A high-volume IoT pipeline needs to run millions of short workflow executions per day as cheaply as possible, and can tolerate at-least-once execution. Which Step Functions type fits?
questions.explanation: Express Workflows are priced per execution/duration for high-volume, short-duration workloads and provide at-least-once semantics, versus Standard's exactly-once but costlier per-transition pricing.

title: Week Synthesis — Compute Decision Matrix & Scenario Drills
summary: Consolidate compute choice criteria: container orchestration (ECS vs EKS), serverless vs server-based, Fargate vs managed nodes, and scaling mechanics. Expect scenario questions that hinge on operational overhead, cost, and control trade-offs.
lab: Complete 15 scenario questions requiring you to choose the right compute platform given constraints (team Kubernetes experience, cost sensitivity, cold-start tolerance).

questions.q: A team has deep existing Kubernetes tooling and multi-cloud portability requirements. Which AWS compute platform best fits?
questions.explanation: EKS runs standard Kubernetes, preserving existing tooling/manifests and easing multi-cloud portability, unlike ECS's AWS-proprietary orchestration model.

title: Amazon Aurora Architecture & Aurora Global Database
summary: Aurora decouples compute from a distributed, self-healing storage layer replicated 6 ways across 3 AZs, giving near-instant crash recovery and fast read replica promotion. Aurora Global Database adds cross-region replication (typically <1s lag) via the storage layer (not binlog), with a secondary region promotable in under a minute for DR.
lab: Simulate an Aurora Global Database managed planned failover and measure the promotion time of the secondary region to primary.

questions.q: A global app needs a secondary region readable with sub-second replication lag and the ability to promote to primary in under a minute during a regional outage. Which database fits?
options: RDS Multi-AZ with a cross-region read replica
RDS read replica with async replication
questions.explanation: Aurora Global Database is purpose-built for this: storage-layer cross-region replication with typical <1s lag and managed failover promoting the secondary in under a minute (RPO/RTO measured in seconds).

title: Amazon RDS Multi-AZ vs Read Replicas & Blue/Green Deployments
summary: Multi-AZ is for HA (synchronous standby, automatic failover, same endpoint) — it does not scale reads. Read replicas (async) scale read throughput and can be promoted to standalone but cause data loss risk on promotion. RDS Blue/Green Deployments create a fully synchronized staging environment for safer major-version upgrades and schema changes, with fast switchover.
lab: Set up an RDS Blue/Green Deployment to test a major-version upgrade against production traffic shape before switchover.

questions.q: A team needs to upgrade RDS MySQL from 5.7 to 8.0 with minimal risk and a fast rollback path. What should they use?
options: In-place major version upgrade during a maintenance window
RDS Blue/Green Deployments to validate on a synced green environment before switchover
questions.explanation: Blue/Green Deployments create a fully replicated green environment on the new version, validated before a fast, low-risk switchover — reducing the blast radius of major upgrades.

title: Amazon DynamoDB Deep Dive — Partitioning & Capacity Modes
summary: DynamoDB partitions data by hash of the partition key; poor key design (low cardinality, hot keys) causes throttling regardless of overall table throughput. On-demand capacity auto-scales per request with no capacity planning (best for unpredictable traffic); provisioned capacity (with auto scaling) is cheaper for steady, predictable workloads.
lab: Redesign a DynamoDB table's partition key from a low-cardinality status field to a composite key that spreads load evenly, eliminating hot-partition throttling.

questions.q: A DynamoDB table using 'OrderStatus' (5 possible values) as the partition key is throttling under high write volume even though total table capacity is high. Why?
options: Low-cardinality partition keys create hot partitions since a partition's throughput is capped regardless of table-level capacity
DynamoDB doesn't support high write volume
questions.explanation: Each partition has its own throughput ceiling; a key with only 5 distinct values concentrates all writes onto a handful of partitions, causing throttling even with ample table-level capacity.

title: DynamoDB Global Tables & DAX Caching
summary: Global Tables provide multi-region, multi-active replication with last-writer-wins conflict resolution — ideal for low-latency global reads/writes without a single-region bottleneck. DAX is an in-memory read-through/write-through cache in front of DynamoDB, cutting read latency from milliseconds to microseconds for read-heavy workloads.
lab: Enable DynamoDB Global Tables across two regions and reason through last-writer-wins conflict behavior for a concurrent update scenario.

questions.q: A gaming leaderboard needs microsecond read latency for the same items requested extremely frequently. What should sit in front of DynamoDB?
options: CloudFront caching of API responses only
DynamoDB Accelerator is not a real service — use RDS instead
questions.explanation: DAX is a managed, DynamoDB-API-compatible in-memory cache purpose-built to shave read latency for hot items without application-level cache logic.

title: Amazon S3 Storage Classes, Lifecycle & Replication
summary: S3 storage classes trade cost for retrieval latency/availability (Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Standard-IA, One Zone-IA, Glacier Instant/Flexible/Deep Archive). Lifecycle rules automate transitions and expirations. Cross-Region Replication (CRR) and Same-Region Replication (SRR) replicate objects asynchronously, commonly for DR or compliance data residency.
lab: Design an S3 lifecycle policy transitioning logs to Standard-IA at 30 days, Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 90 days, and expiring them at 400 days.

questions.q: An object needs the lowest storage cost, is rarely accessed, and a 12-hour retrieval time is acceptable, but it must survive loss of an entire AZ.
questions.explanation: Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost class, replicated across 3+ AZs (so it survives an AZ loss, unlike One Zone-IA), with retrieval times up to 12 hours matching the requirement.

title: Amazon ElastiCache — Redis vs Memcached Architectures
summary: Redis supports replication, persistence, pub/sub, and cluster mode sharding, plus Global Datastore for cross-region replication — choose it whenever HA, durability, or complex data structures matter. Memcached is purely a simple, multi-threaded, non-persistent cache for horizontally scaled, stateless caching with no replication.
lab: Compare ElastiCache Redis cluster mode (sharded, replicated) against Memcached for a session-store use case requiring failover.

questions.q: A session store must survive a node failure without losing data and support automatic failover. Which caching engine and configuration fits?
options: Redis with cluster mode enabled and replicas per shard
questions.explanation: Only Redis supports replication and automatic failover; Memcached has no replication and node failure means data loss for those keys.

title: Week Synthesis — Database Selection Matrix & Scenario Drills
summary: Consolidate database/storage selection: relational vs key-value vs cache, consistency models, and global replication trade-offs (Aurora Global DB vs DynamoDB Global Tables). This is a heavily tested exam domain.
lab: Complete 15 scenario questions requiring justification of a database choice against stated latency, consistency, and scale requirements.

questions.q: An application needs single-digit-millisecond reads/writes at massive unpredictable scale with a flexible schema, across multiple regions actively writing. What fits best?
options: ElastiCache alone as the system of record
questions.explanation: DynamoDB Global Tables provide multi-active, multi-region writes at single-digit-millisecond latency with a flexible schema — a fit that Aurora Global DB (single writer region) and RDS replicas don't match.

title: CloudWatch Metrics, Alarms & Composite Alarms
summary: CloudWatch alarms trigger on metric thresholds (static or ML-based anomaly detection bands); composite alarms combine multiple alarm states with AND/OR logic to reduce alert noise and only page when a true incident pattern occurs (e.g. high latency AND high error rate together).
lab: Build a composite alarm that only fires when both high latency and elevated 5xx error rate alarms are ALARM simultaneously, suppressing single-metric noise.

questions.q: On-call engineers are fatigued by alarms firing on isolated latency spikes that self-resolve. What reduces noise while still catching real incidents?
options: A composite alarm requiring both the latency alarm AND the error-rate alarm to be in ALARM state
Increase the evaluation period to 24 hours
questions.explanation: Composite alarms let you require correlated signals before paging, cutting single-metric false positives while preserving sensitivity to genuine multi-symptom incidents.

title: CloudWatch Synthetics & Canaries for SLO Monitoring
summary: Synthetics canaries are scripted (Puppeteer/Selenium-based) probes that continuously exercise your endpoints/user flows from outside your infrastructure, catching availability and latency SLO breaches before real users report them — complementary to internal metrics.
lab: Create a canary that logs into the application and completes a checkout flow every 5 minutes, alarming on failure or latency SLO breach.

questions.q: Internal CloudWatch metrics show healthy servers, but customers report the login page is broken. What monitoring gap does this reveal?
options: No outside-in synthetic monitoring of the actual user flow
questions.explanation: Server-side health metrics don't verify end-to-end user experience; Synthetics canaries probe from outside the infrastructure, catching failures (DNS, CDN, front-end bugs) invisible to internal metrics.

title: AWS X-Ray Distributed Tracing
summary: X-Ray traces a request across microservices, building a service map that highlights latency and error hotspots per hop. Sampling rules control trace volume/cost, and annotations/subsegments let you filter and drill into specific downstream calls (e.g. a slow DynamoDB query inside a Lambda invocation).
lab: Instrument a Lambda-to-DynamoDB call chain with X-Ray and identify which downstream hop contributes most to p99 latency using the service map.

questions.q: A microservices app has growing p99 latency but it's unclear which of 12 services is the bottleneck. What AWS service pinpoints this?
options: AWS X-Ray, using the service map to isolate the slow hop
questions.explanation: X-Ray's distributed tracing and service map visualize per-hop latency across the full call chain, directly identifying the bottleneck service that aggregate metrics can't isolate.

title: Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights & Centralized Logging
summary: Logs Insights provides a query language over CloudWatch Logs for ad-hoc analysis without standing up separate infrastructure. Subscription filters stream logs in real time to a centralized logging account (via Kinesis Data Firehose/Streams) for org-wide search, retention, and SIEM ingestion.
lab: Write a Logs Insights query extracting the top 10 slowest API requests in the last hour, then configure a subscription filter to forward ERROR-level logs to a central account.

questions.q: An organization wants every account's application logs centrally searchable in a dedicated logging account in near-real time. What's the mechanism?
options: Manually export logs nightly via S3
CloudWatch Logs subscription filters streaming to Kinesis Data Firehose in the central logging account
Increase log retention in each account
questions.explanation: Subscription filters push log events in near-real time to a destination (commonly Kinesis Firehose/Streams) in a centralized account, enabling org-wide log aggregation.

title: AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) — Chaos Engineering Fundamentals
summary: FIS runs controlled chaos experiments (EC2/ECS/EKS termination, CPU/network stress, RDS/AZ failover) defined as experiment templates with mandatory stop conditions tied to CloudWatch alarms, automatically halting the experiment if it threatens production stability.
lab: Execute an FIS experiment terminating a random ECS task and verify the service self-heals within its target RTO, with a stop condition tied to an error-rate alarm.

questions.q: A team wants to safely test EC2 instance failure in production without risking an uncontrolled outage. What FIS feature guarantees the experiment halts if things go wrong?
options: Stop conditions tied to CloudWatch alarms
questions.explanation: FIS stop conditions automatically abort a running experiment the moment a linked CloudWatch alarm enters ALARM state, capping the blast radius of chaos testing.

title: Designing Game Days & Chaos Experiments
summary: A Game Day is a scheduled exercise simulating a real failure (AZ outage, dependency failure, region loss) to validate that runbooks, alarms, and automated recovery actually work under realistic conditions — turning DR assumptions into tested facts.
lab: Design a Game Day script simulating full AZ failure for a 3-AZ application, defining success criteria (RTO/RPO targets) in advance.

questions.q: A team has documented DR runbooks but has never tested them under simulated failure. What is the recommended next step before relying on them?
options: Run a Game Day exercise using FIS to simulate the failure and validate the runbook and automated recovery actually work
Skip testing to avoid production risk
questions.explanation: Untested runbooks are unverified assumptions; a Game Day exercises the real failure mode against real infrastructure to confirm RTO/RPO targets are actually achievable.

title: Multi-Region Active-Active Architectures
summary: Active-active serves live traffic from 2+ regions simultaneously, requiring multi-region data replication with conflict resolution (DynamoDB Global Tables, or careful partitioning), and global traffic steering via Route 53 latency/geoproximity routing or Global Accelerator's anycast IPs for fast failover at the network layer.
lab: Design an active-active architecture using Global Accelerator for traffic steering and DynamoDB Global Tables for data, reasoning through conflict resolution.

questions.q: An active-active app needs sub-second failover at the network layer when a region's health checks fail, independent of DNS TTL/caching issues.
options: AWS Global Accelerator, which uses static anycast IPs and reroutes at the AWS network edge instantly
questions.explanation: Global Accelerator uses anycast IPs and AWS's global network for near-instant failover, avoiding client-side DNS caching delays inherent to Route 53-only failover.

title: Multi-Region Active-Passive & Pilot Light Patterns
summary: DR strategies form a cost/RTO spectrum: Backup & Restore (cheapest, highest RTO/RPO, hours-days), Pilot Light (core data replicated, minimal standby infra, RTO ~10s of minutes), Warm Standby (scaled-down full replica running, RTO minutes), and Multi-Site Active-Active (lowest RTO/RPO, highest cost).
lab: Map a workload's business RTO/RPO requirement to the cheapest DR strategy on the spectrum that satisfies it, and justify the choice.

questions.q: A workload can tolerate an RTO of 15 minutes and RPO of 5 minutes, but the business wants to minimize standing infrastructure cost. Which DR pattern fits best?
questions.explanation: Pilot Light keeps only core data continuously replicated and minimal infrastructure running, scaling up the rest on failover — matching a ~15-minute RTO at much lower cost than warm standby or active-active.

title: Route 53 Application Recovery Controller (ARC)
summary: Route 53 ARC provides readiness checks (continuously validating a standby region actually has capacity/config to take over) and routing controls with a highly available control plane (independent of a single region) for deterministic, auditable failover — safer than ad hoc Route 53 health-check failover for critical systems.
lab: Configure ARC readiness checks validating that a standby region's Auto Scaling Group capacity matches production before it's considered a valid failover target.

questions.q: A critical financial system needs failover control that itself won't fail if an entire AWS region goes down, plus proof the standby region is actually ready to serve traffic.
options: Route 53 Application Recovery Controller (readiness checks + a highly available routing control cluster)
CloudWatch Alarms triggering a Lambda failover
questions.explanation: ARC's routing control cluster is deliberately distributed across regions/partitions for resilience of the failover mechanism itself, and readiness checks validate standby capacity before you rely on it.

title: Route 53 Routing Policies & Health Checks
summary: Route 53 supports simple, weighted (canary/A-B), latency-based, failover, geolocation, geoproximity (with bias), and multi-value answer routing — each paired with health checks that automatically remove unhealthy endpoints from DNS responses.
lab: Configure weighted routing to shift 5% of traffic to a canary deployment, combined with a health check that automatically pulls it from rotation on failure.

questions.q: You want most users routed to the AWS region with the lowest network latency for them, automatically.
questions.explanation: Latency-based routing uses AWS's latency measurements between users and regions to route each request to the lowest-latency healthy endpoint.

title: RTO/RPO Design Patterns & Backup Strategies (AWS Backup)
summary: AWS Backup centralizes policy-based backup (schedules, lifecycle, cross-region and cross-account copy) across EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS, and more, from one console. Vault Lock enforces WORM (write-once-read-many) immutability for compliance and ransomware protection.
lab: Create an AWS Backup plan with daily backups, cross-account copy to an isolated backup account, and a locked vault preventing deletion even by admins.

questions.q: A company needs ransomware-resilient backups that cannot be deleted even by a compromised admin account. What should they configure?
options: AWS Backup with a cross-account copy into an isolated account, in a vault with Backup Vault Lock enabled
questions.explanation: Cross-account isolation prevents a compromised primary account from touching backups, and Vault Lock makes the retention policy immutable — even the root user can't delete locked backups before expiry.

title: Well-Architected Reliability Pillar Deep Dive
summary: The Reliability pillar centers on foundations (service quotas, network topology), workload architecture (distributed system design, graceful degradation), change management (automated deployment, monitoring), and failure management (backup, DR, tested recovery procedures).
lab: Run a Reliability pillar review against a sample architecture, identifying single points of failure and missing automated recovery.

questions.q: Which best exemplifies the Reliability pillar's 'failure management' best practice?
options: Using the largest possible instance type
Automatically testing recovery procedures via Game Days and setting quantified RTO/RPO targets
questions.explanation: Failure management is about anticipating failure, testing recovery (Game Days), and having quantified, validated RTO/RPO — not just provisioning bigger resources.

title: Well-Architected Operational Excellence Pillar
summary: Operational Excellence emphasizes performing operations as code (IaC, automated runbooks/playbooks), making frequent small reversible changes, anticipating failure through game days, and learning from operational events via blameless post-incident reviews.
lab: Convert a manual runbook step into an automated SSM Automation document, reducing human-triggered operational error.

questions.q: A team manually SSHes into servers to apply emergency patches, occasionally causing config drift. Which Operational Excellence practice addresses this?
options: Perform operations as code using SSM Automation documents/runbooks instead of manual SSH changes
questions.explanation: 'Operations as code' — codifying operational procedures (e.g. SSM Automation) — eliminates ad hoc manual changes and the drift/error they introduce.

title: Week Synthesis — SRE & DR Scenario Drills
summary: Consolidate observability (metrics, tracing, synthetics), chaos engineering, and DR pattern selection (backup/restore through active-active). This SRE cluster is central to the exam's resilience domain.
lab: Complete 20 scenario questions requiring you to select the correct DR pattern and observability tool given a stated RTO/RPO and budget.

questions.q: A workload requires near-zero RTO/RPO and budget is not the primary constraint. Which DR strategy and supporting service pairing fits?
options: Pilot Light with manual DNS updates
Multi-Site Active-Active with Route 53 ARC and DynamoDB Global Tables/Aurora Global Database
questions.explanation: Near-zero RTO/RPO demands live traffic serving from multiple regions (active-active) with deterministic, tested failover control (ARC) and multi-region-write-capable data services.

title: Migration Strategy Framework — The 7 Rs & Migration Hub
services: 7 Rs (Retire, Retain, Rehost, Relocate, Repurchase, Replatform, Refactor)
summary: The 7 Rs classify how to move each workload: Retire (decommission), Retain (keep as-is for now), Rehost (lift-and-shift, e.g. via MGN), Relocate (move VMware workloads to VMware Cloud on AWS unchanged), Repurchase (move to SaaS), Replatform (lift-tinker-and-shift, e.g. self-managed MySQL to RDS), and Refactor (re-architect to cloud-native). Migration Hub centrally tracks progress across tools.
lab: Classify a portfolio of 10 sample applications into the correct 'R' strategy based on stated business constraints (deadline, licensing, technical debt).

questions.q: A data center lease expires in 6 months, forcing a fast migration, but two legacy apps have unresolved software licensing blockers. What's the correct 7 Rs plan?
options: Rehost the majority via MGN to meet the deadline; Retain the two blocked apps until licensing is resolved
questions.explanation: Under a tight deadline, Rehost (lift-and-shift) is the fastest path for most apps; apps with real blockers should be explicitly Retained rather than forced into a rushed migration.

title: AWS Application Discovery Service — Assessment & Portfolio Analysis
summary: Application Discovery Service (agent-based or agentless) inventories on-prem servers, dependencies, and utilization data to build a data-driven migration plan and right-size target instances, feeding into Migration Hub for tracking.
lab: Review how agentless discovery (via a VM export/OVA) differs from agent-based discovery for capturing process-level network dependencies.

questions.q: A migration team needs to map network dependencies between individual processes on each server before planning application groupings for migration waves. What captures this?
options: Agent-based discovery, which captures process-to-process network connections
questions.explanation: Agent-based discovery installs a lightweight agent per server and captures fine-grained, process-level network connections — agentless discovery only gives VM-level inventory/utilization.

title: AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) — Lift-and-Shift Rehost
summary: MGN performs continuous, low-impact block-level replication from source servers (physical, VM, or other clouds) to a staging area in AWS, letting you launch test and cutover instances at any point with minimal downtime — replacing the older CloudEndure/SMS workflow as the standard AWS rehost tool.
lab: Install the MGN replication agent on a source server, launch a non-disruptive test instance, then perform a cutover with a short maintenance window.

questions.q: A company needs to rehost 200 on-prem VMs to EC2 as fast as possible with minimal application changes and minimal cutover downtime.
questions.explanation: MGN is purpose-built for server rehost: continuous replication lets you test extensively and cut over with just minutes of downtime, without re-architecting the application.

title: AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) — Heterogeneous Schema Conversion
summary: SCT converts database schema, views, stored procedures, and functions when migrating between different engines (e.g. Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL). It reports a conversion-completeness percentage, but even a high percentage (e.g. 95%) leaves complex procedural code requiring manual remediation. SCT handles schema; AWS DMS handles the data itself.
lab: Run SCT against a sample Oracle schema with stored procedures, review the generated conversion action report, and identify objects needing manual rework.

questions.q: SCT reports a 92% automatic conversion rate for an Oracle-to-PostgreSQL migration. What does this mean for the remaining 8%?
options: The migration is essentially complete and can proceed unattended
Complex objects like certain stored procedures/functions couldn't be auto-converted and need manual developer remediation before cutover
SCT failed and DMS cannot be used
8% of the data will be lost during migration
questions.explanation: SCT's conversion percentage reflects schema/code objects only; a high percentage still commonly leaves complex procedural logic that must be manually rewritten before the heterogeneous migration is production-ready.

title: AWS DataSync — Hybrid File & Object Transfer
summary: DataSync automates and accelerates online transfer of files/objects between on-prem storage (NFS, SMB, HDFS, self-managed object storage) and AWS storage (S3, EFS, FSx), with built-in scheduling, encryption, bandwidth throttling, and data integrity validation — unlike DMS, it is not database-aware.
lab: Configure a DataSync task migrating an on-prem NFS share to S3 on a nightly schedule with bandwidth throttling to protect production network capacity.

questions.q: A company needs to continuously sync a large on-prem NFS file share into Amazon EFS, on a schedule, without writing custom scripts.
questions.explanation: DataSync is purpose-built for automated, scheduled, validated file/object transfer between on-prem file systems and AWS storage services like EFS, FSx, and S3.

title: AWS Storage Gateway — File, Volume & Tape Gateways
summary: File Gateway presents S3 as an NFS/SMB share with local caching for low-latency access to hot data. Volume Gateway provides iSCSI block storage backed by S3, in cached (primary data in S3, hot data cached locally) or stored (primary data on-prem, async backup to S3) modes. Tape Gateway is a virtual tape library (VTL) replacing physical backup tape infrastructure.
lab: Compare cached vs stored Volume Gateway modes for an on-prem application requiring low-latency local reads but durable cloud backup.

questions.q: An enterprise wants to eliminate its physical backup tape infrastructure while keeping existing backup software unchanged.
questions.explanation: Tape Gateway presents a virtual tape library interface compatible with existing backup software, letting you retire physical tape hardware without changing backup workflows.

title: AWS Snow Family — Snowball Edge, Snowcone & Snowmobile
summary: The Snow Family moves large datasets offline when network transfer would take too long or is unavailable: Snowcone (small, edge/rugged use), Snowball Edge (Storage Optimized up to ~80TB usable, or Compute Optimized with GPU for edge processing), and Snowmobile (exabyte-scale, shipping-container data center on wheels).
lab: Calculate whether a 500TB one-time transfer over a 100Mbps link (theoretical ~46 days) justifies using Snowball Edge instead, and size the number of devices needed.

questions.q: A company must migrate 2 PB of data from a facility with no viable network uplink for bulk transfer. What is the appropriate approach?
options: Multiple AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized devices (or Snowmobile for the full 2PB in one engagement)
questions.explanation: At petabyte scale with no adequate network path, physical offline transfer via Snow Family devices (Snowball Edge in bulk, or Snowmobile for exabyte-scale single engagements) is the standard, cost-effective solution.

title: Hybrid Cloud Compute — Outposts, Local Zones & Wavelength
summary: Outposts extends AWS infrastructure and APIs into your own data center for workloads needing local data residency or ultra-low latency to on-prem systems. Local Zones place AWS compute/storage in specific metro areas for low-latency access without owning hardware. Wavelength embeds AWS compute at telco 5G network edges for ultra-low-latency mobile applications.
lab: Decide between Outposts, a Local Zone, and Wavelength for a manufacturing plant requiring single-digit-millisecond latency to on-prem industrial control systems.

questions.q: A hospital must keep patient data physically on-premises for regulatory reasons while still using native AWS APIs (EC2, EBS, RDS on Outposts) for its applications.
questions.explanation: Outposts physically places AWS-managed infrastructure inside the customer's own data center, satisfying strict data-residency requirements while retaining native AWS service APIs.

title: VMware Cloud on AWS — Relocate Strategy
summary: The Relocate strategy migrates VMware-virtualized workloads to VMware Cloud on AWS without converting them to native EC2/AMI format, preserving the existing hypervisor layer and VMware tooling — used when organizations want cloud infrastructure benefits without an application-level re-platform, often as an interim step before eventual native refactor.
lab: Compare a Relocate (VMware Cloud on AWS via HCX) approach against a Rehost (MGN to native EC2) approach for a VM the team doesn't want to convert.

questions.q: A team wants to move VMware VMs to AWS infrastructure fastest, keeping the exact same hypervisor-level configuration and VMware management tools, with no P2V/V2V conversion.
questions.explanation: Relocate via VMware Cloud on AWS is the only 7 Rs strategy that moves the VM without converting it out of the VMware format, unlike Rehost which lands on native EC2/AMIs.

title: Direct Connect Capacity Planning for Large-Scale Migration
summary: For sustained large-scale migration traffic, provision Direct Connect capacity (or LAG-bundled connections for higher aggregate throughput) ahead of the migration window, and consider temporarily using Snowball for the bulk historical dataset while DX/DMS CDC handles the ongoing delta — hybrid transfer strategies are common on the exam.
lab: Calculate whether a planned migration's data volume and timeline justify provisioning additional Direct Connect capacity versus a one-time Snowball bulk transfer plus CDC delta sync.

questions.q: A migration needs to move 300TB of historical data plus ongoing daily deltas of ~50GB, with a network link capped at 500 Mbps.
options: Transfer everything, including historical data, over the 500 Mbps link
Use Snowball Edge for the 300TB bulk historical transfer, then DMS CDC (or DataSync) over the network link for ongoing deltas
Wait for the network link to be upgraded before starting
Use Snowmobile for the entire migration
questions.explanation: This hybrid pattern — offline bulk transfer for the large historical dataset, then network-based CDC/incremental sync for the small ongoing delta — is a standard, exam-tested approach to large migrations over constrained links.

title: Cost Optimization — Savings Plans, RIs & Spot Fleet Strategy
summary: Compute Savings Plans offer the most flexibility (any instance family/region/OS) for a 1-3yr commitment; EC2 Instance Savings Plans are cheaper but locked to an instance family/region. Reserved Instances add capacity reservation options. Spot Instances (up to ~90% discount) suit fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads, paired with Spot Fleet/mixed-instance ASGs for diversified capacity and graceful 2-minute interruption handling.
lab: Design a mixed-instance Auto Scaling Group combining On-Demand baseline capacity with Spot Fleet for burst capacity, using a Spot interruption handler.

questions.q: A company runs a steady-state, predictable production fleet but wants maximum flexibility to change instance families and regions over the commitment period.
questions.explanation: Compute Savings Plans apply across any instance family, region, OS, and even Fargate/Lambda usage, trading a slightly lower discount than EC2 Instance Savings Plans for maximum flexibility.

title: AWS Compute Optimizer, Cost Explorer & Trusted Advisor
summary: Compute Optimizer analyzes utilization metrics and recommends right-sizing (often catching over-provisioned instances). Cost Explorer visualizes spend trends and forecasts, supporting RI/Savings Plan purchase recommendations. Trusted Advisor flags cost, security, performance, and fault-tolerance issues against AWS best practices.
lab: Use Compute Optimizer recommendations to identify and right-size the top 5 most over-provisioned EC2 instances in a sample fleet.

questions.q: A company suspects many EC2 instances are oversized relative to actual CPU/memory utilization but doesn't know which ones. What AWS service directly recommends right-sizing changes?
options: AWS Trusted Advisor cost checks only
questions.explanation: Compute Optimizer analyzes historical utilization and provides specific instance-type right-sizing recommendations with projected savings, more targeted than Trusted Advisor's general cost checks.

title: FinOps on AWS — Tagging, Budgets & Cost Allocation Reports
summary: Consistent resource tagging (enforced via SCPs/Config rules) enables cost allocation reports that attribute spend by team/project/environment. AWS Budgets alerts on forecasted or actual overspend; the Cost and Usage Report (CUR) provides the most granular billing data for custom BI/FinOps tooling.
lab: Design a mandatory tagging policy (enforced via SCP) requiring CostCenter and Environment tags on all resource creation, then build a Budget alert per cost center.

questions.q: Finance wants to see AWS spend broken out per business unit, but resources are inconsistently tagged today. What should be enforced first?
options: Enforce a mandatory tagging policy (e.g. via SCP/Config) requiring cost-allocation tags at resource creation, then activate those tags for cost allocation reporting
Use a single shared account for all business units
Manually track spend in a spreadsheet
questions.explanation: Cost allocation reporting is only as good as tag hygiene; enforcing mandatory tags at creation time (via SCP or Config rules) is the prerequisite before per-business-unit cost reports become meaningful.

title: AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) — Homogeneous & Heterogeneous Migration with CDC
summary: TODAY'S FOCUS. Full detailed lesson below — this is one of the highest-yield topics on the exam (3-4 questions typically), covering DMS architecture, full load vs CDC, replication instance sizing, LOB handling, and the DMS+SCT heterogeneous migration pattern.
lab: See full hands-on lab and 15 scenario questions below.

title: Full-Length Mock Exam 1 — 75 Questions Timed
summary: Take a complete 75-question, 180-minute timed mock exam under real exam conditions (no pausing, no notes) to establish a baseline score and get comfortable with SAP-C02 pacing (~2.4 minutes/question average, though scenario questions need more).
lab: Complete one full 180-minute timed mock exam without interruption; do not review answers until finished.

questions.q: On the real SAP-C02 exam, roughly how much time should you budget per question on average to finish 75 questions in 180 minutes with review time left over?
options: About 2-2.5 minutes per question, flagging longer scenario questions for a second pass
questions.explanation: 180 minutes / 75 questions is 2.4 minutes average; the standard technique is to answer straightforward questions quickly, flag long scenarios, and return to flagged questions with remaining time.

title: Mock Exam 1 Distractor Analysis & Weak Domain Review
summary: Review every missed question, but more importantly review questions you answered correctly by luck or elimination — for each, articulate *why* the correct answer is right and *why each distractor* is wrong. Tag each miss by domain to find your weakest area.
lab: For every incorrect answer, write one sentence explaining why the correct option is right and one sentence per distractor explaining why it's wrong.

questions.q: Why is analyzing wrong-but-eliminated distractors as valuable as reviewing missed questions?
options: It isn't valuable, only review misses
Distractors are designed around common misconceptions; understanding why they're wrong hardens your understanding of edge cases the exam repeatedly tests
questions.explanation: SAP-C02 distractors are deliberately plausible-sounding services/configurations; explicitly naming why each is wrong closes the exact conceptual gaps the exam is designed to probe.

title: Deep Review — Domain 1 Weak Areas (Org/Governance/Networking)
summary: Revisit Weeks 1-2 content (multi-account governance and hybrid networking) focused specifically on whatever domain analysis from Day 58 flagged as weak.
lab: Re-do all missed Week 1-2 practice questions from Days 1-14, plus 10 new scenario questions targeting your weakest sub-topic.

title: Deep Review — Domain 2 Weak Areas (Resilient Architectures)
summary: Revisit Weeks 3-6 content (compute, databases, SRE/DR) focused on flagged weak areas from mock exam analysis.
lab: Re-do all missed Week 3-6 practice questions from Days 15-42, plus 10 new scenario questions targeting your weakest sub-topic.

title: Full-Length Mock Exam 2 — 75 Questions Timed
summary: Second full timed mock exam. Compare score delta against Mock Exam 1 to measure whether the Day 59-60 deep review closed the gaps it targeted.
lab: Complete one full 180-minute timed mock exam without interruption.

title: Mock Exam 2 Distractor Analysis & Weak Domain Review
summary: Repeat the Day 58 distractor-analysis process for Mock Exam 2, tracking whether previously weak domains have improved or if new gaps emerged.
lab: For every incorrect answer, write out why the correct option is right and why each distractor is wrong; re-tag domain weak spots.

title: Deep Review — Domain 3 Weak Areas (Migration & Modernization)
summary: Revisit Week 7-8 migration content (the 7 Rs, MGN, DMS/SCT, DataSync, Snow Family, hybrid networking capacity) focused on flagged weak areas.
lab: Re-do all missed Week 7-8 practice questions from Days 43-56, plus 10 new scenario questions targeting your weakest sub-topic.

title: Deep Review — Domain 4 Weak Areas (Cost Control)
summary: Revisit cost optimization content (Savings Plans vs RIs vs Spot, Compute Optimizer, FinOps tagging/budgets) focused on flagged weak areas.
lab: Re-do all missed cost-optimization practice questions, plus 10 new scenario questions on Savings Plans vs Reserved Instance selection.

title: Full-Length Mock Exam 3 — 75 Questions Timed
summary: Third full timed mock exam. By this point your score should be trending toward the 80%+ target range consistently.
lab: Complete one full 180-minute timed mock exam without interruption.

title: Mock Exam 3 Distractor Analysis & Timing/Pacing Strategy
summary: Beyond content review, analyze your time-per-question data: which question types cost you the most time, and refine your flag-and-skip strategy accordingly.
lab: Track time spent per question on Mock Exam 3; identify the 10 slowest questions and diagnose whether the delay was content gaps or overthinking.

title: Full-Length Mock Exam 4 — 75 Questions Timed
summary: Fourth full timed mock exam, ideally from a different question bank/vendor than exams 1-3 to reduce pattern memorization and test genuine understanding.
lab: Complete one full 180-minute timed mock exam without interruption, using a different practice exam provider if possible.

title: Mock Exam 4 Distractor Analysis & Flag-and-Review Technique
summary: Final full distractor analysis pass. Refine the flag-and-review technique: which questions do you consistently need a second look at, and why.
lab: Complete distractor analysis; write a one-page personal 'weak spot cheat sheet' to review the morning of the exam.

title: Full-Length Mock Exam 5 — 75 Questions Timed
summary: Fifth and final full timed mock exam. Target consistently scoring above 85% before sitting the real exam.
lab: Complete the final full 180-minute timed mock exam without interruption.

title: Final Review — Exam Day Logistics, Pearson VUE Checklist & Confidence Drills
summary: Light review only — re-read your personal weak-spot cheat sheet, confirm Pearson VUE/OnVUE logistics (ID requirements, room scan for online proctoring, check-in time), and avoid cramming new material the day before the exam.
lab: Confirm exam appointment details, prepare valid ID, do a final light pass of the personal cheat sheet built on Day 68, and get a full night's sleep.

questions.q: The day before the SAP-C02 exam, what is the most effective use of study time?
options: Cram as many new topics as possible
Light review of your personal weak-spot cheat sheet, logistics confirmation, and rest — not new material
Take a 6th full mock exam back-to-back
questions.explanation: By the final day, marginal new learning is low-value and risks fatigue/anxiety; reviewing known weak spots lightly and ensuring logistics/rest are handled has the best return on exam-day performance.
